profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting between a faculty lead and a postdoctoral researcher preparing the next six weeks of work for a follow-up ML study on interpretable clinical decision-support systems for heart-failure risk prediction. They need to align on the pilot build for an RL-based DSS that learns which explanation sequences increase clinician confidence, finalize what goes into the IRB amendment, decide which interface will serve as the control condition, define the first internal milestone, and assign owners for code, study materials, and outreach. The expected outcome is an apparently shared execution plan for getting the pilot system, study package, and clinician-facing materials 'ready,' even though several second-order assumptions about scope, artifacts, and readiness remain misaligned.

members.name: Dr. Maya Rangan
members.expertise: ML interpretability, human-centered evaluation, clinical AI study design
members.background: An associate professor who leads a lab on interpretable machine learning in healthcare and has run several clinician-facing studies involving IRB protocols, cross-institution collaborators, and paper-ready experimental framing.
members.private_state: She wants the follow-up study to look methodologically clean and low-risk in the amendment and upcoming progress report, and she is trying to avoid any engineering dependency that could delay clinician feedback or force changes to the study narrative.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pilot build' can legitimately include Wizard-of-Oz or manually triggered components as long as the clinician-facing flow is stable and the observed interaction is the one described in the study materials.

The 'baseline interface' naturally means the previously used control condition from the earlier heart-failure study because that is the baseline that matters for continuity, writeup, and IRB language.
'Pilot users' refers to the lab's internal clinical advisory board—3 to 5 known clinicians who will tolerate glitches and participate in moderated sessions.

When the team says 'freeze the model,' the frozen object is the heart-failure risk predictor; the explanation-selection policy can still be tuned offline because she sees it as part of the surrounding interface logic, not the core predictive model.
A Friday handoff means a reviewable package in her inbox by end of day local time, polished enough to circulate to collaborators without caveats.

members.name: Dr. Leo Martinez
members.expertise: Reinforcement learning, interactive ML systems, experimental infrastructure
members.background: A recently hired postdoc from an industry research lab who specializes in adaptive interfaces and end-to-end experimentation, with strong engineering instincts and less experience with how clinical pilot studies are often staged through advisory users and protocol-friendly simplifications.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid building throwaway prototypes and is pushing to make the pilot stack reusable for the full study, with genuine online behavior, logging, and deployment conventions that will not need reimplementation later.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pilot build' should be the same technical pathway intended for the real study, including automated policy calls, persistent logging, and no hidden manual intervention, because otherwise pilot behavior is not representative.
The 'baseline interface' means the maintained spring dashboard branch used in the lab demo, since that is the only baseline implementation he considers current and supportable.

'Pilot users' means the first recruited clinicians who fit the study's target participant profile, even if the batch is small, so the system should be usable asynchronously without a team member driving the session.
When the team says 'freeze the model,' that includes both the predictor and the RL policy because the full DSS behavior is what generates the study data.
A Friday deadline means code merged by Friday night UTC, with documentation cleanup and collaborator-facing packaging able to happen afterward.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the pilot build
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'get the pilot build ready' before opening the next phase.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a clinician-facing pilot flow that appears complete during sessions, even if the explanation sequence is partly advanced manually from a researcher console and some backend events are captured through lightweight scripts.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a technically complete end-to-end build in which the RL policy selects explanation cards automatically, all events are logged through the production-style pipeline, and no hidden human intervention is needed.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are talking about the same screens and study flow, so the phrase 'pilot build' sounds fully shared; the disagreement is only about invisible backend completeness, which each treats as the obvious standard and therefore never foregrounds.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'keep the baseline interface as the control condition.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the prior heart-failure control condition used in the earlier study: a static risk score, short feature-importance card, and confidence indicator presented on a single review screen.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the spring demo dashboard branch: a cleaned-up interface with trend panels, grouped features, and collapsible rationale sections, but without adaptive sequencing.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Inside the lab, 'the baseline interface' sounds like a uniquely identified artifact, and both versions are familiar enough that neither expects the other to be pointing to a different one.

misalignment_points.topic: Who counts as the pilot users
misalignment_points.surface_form: They say the system should be 'ready for the pilot users' next week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes that 'pilot users' are the internal clinical advisors already informally lined up—cardiologists and hospitalists who know the project and will join moderated Zoom sessions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes that 'pilot users' are the first small batch of formally recruited external clinicians covered by the amendment, using the system on their own schedule.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'pilot users' sounds like established project shorthand rather than something requiring definition, and both assume the relevant user set has already been implicitly fixed elsewhere.

misalignment_points.topic: What exactly gets frozen before sessions
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'freeze the model' before any clinician sessions start.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means freezing the neural network that outputs heart-failure risk predictions, while leaving room to adjust the RL explanation policy or ordering logic during pilot tuning.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means freezing the entire DSS behavior, including both the predictor and the RL policy, so that pilot data are generated under the same configuration intended for the study.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML meetings, 'the model' is often used loosely; M1 centers the predictive network while M2 centers the full interactive system, so the shared phrase creates false consensus without sounding ambiguous.

turns.inner_thought: I need a six-week plan that protects the amendment and the progress report: stable clinician-facing flow, minimal risk, and no dependence on engineering finishing every backend detail. If we can get the pilot build ready in a way that looks complete during moderated advisory sessions, that is enough to start learning from clinicians and keep the study narrative clean.
turns.utterance: Okay, let’s make this concrete. Over the next six weeks, I want us to get the pilot build ready, get the amendment submitted, and line up the first clinician interactions so we’re not still sorting scope at the end of the month.

turns.inner_thought: If the pilot build is supposed to matter, it should be the real technical pathway: automated policy calls, proper event logging, persistent state, deployable service boundaries. I do not want to build a one-off prototype and then throw it away before the actual study.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I’d sequence the work around the policy service, the logging layer, and the deployment path so the pilot build is ready in the right order, and then the rest can sit on top of that.

turns.inner_thought: We should not reopen the control. The baseline interface should mean the prior heart-failure control condition from the earlier study, because that is what gives us continuity in the amendment and eventual writeup.
turns.utterance: Yes. And on the study side, I think we should keep the baseline interface as the control condition. That will make the amendment and the comparison much more straightforward.

turns.inner_thought: Good, so the baseline interface is the spring dashboard branch. That’s the only current implementation I’d want to support anyway, and most of the pieces are already there if I just clean them up.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I can clean up the baseline interface pretty quickly, since most of those pieces already exist and just need tightening up.

turns.inner_thought: By next week, I want something usable with our internal clinical advisory board. Three to five known clinicians, moderated sessions, tolerable if we have to guide the interaction a bit. Ready for the pilot users just means ready to start those conversations.
turns.utterance: Good. I also want the system ready for the pilot users next week so we can start getting reactions to the explanation sequence sooner rather than later.

turns.inner_thought: If pilot users are the first recruited clinicians, the system has to stand on its own without someone driving every click. I should focus on the parts that make first use stable and understandable for asynchronous sessions.
turns.utterance: Right, and if it needs to be ready for the pilot users next week, I should prioritize making the session flow robust and user-friendly ahead of some of the nicer-to-have polish.

turns.inner_thought: I should signal that I’m fine with a lighter initial build. What matters is that clinicians see the intended outputs in the intended order during moderated advisory sessions. If some explanation steps are advanced manually behind the scenes, that is still a valid pilot build for this stage.
turns.utterance: That sounds fine. I’m comfortable with a lighter initial build as long as the clinician-facing flow is stable and the pilot users see the intended outputs in the right order.

turns.inner_thought: I hear that she wants the first pass lean, but I still want to implement the real automation path now. Then the same stack will support the adaptive arm and the baseline interface later, instead of forcing a rebuild.
turns.utterance: Yes, and once that path is in place, the same stack can support both the adaptive arm and the baseline interface without us having to redo everything later.

turns.inner_thought: For the amendment, I need to be able to say the heart-failure predictor is fixed before clinician sessions. That keeps the protocol narrative clean. I’m not worried about still tuning explanation ordering outside the predictor as long as the study-facing language stays simple.
turns.utterance: One thing I want to be explicit about: we should freeze the model before any clinician sessions start, so the protocol narrative stays clean while I’m drafting the amendment language.

turns.inner_thought: Right, freeze the whole system behavior before pilot data collection. I should do one more round of policy tuning now, then lock both predictor and policy so the pilot reflects the final intended configuration.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I’ll do one last round of tuning this week so everything is locked in before sessions start.

turns.inner_thought: I’ll handle the collaborator-facing materials and anything tied to the amendment: consent wording, outreach email, vignette revisions. He can own the pilot build and control-condition package. I need something in my inbox by end of day Friday, polished enough to circulate without a lot of caveats.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I’ll take the consent wording, the outreach email, and the vignette revisions. Can you own the pilot build and the control-condition handoff? If so, let’s aim for a Friday handoff so I can stitch the package together before the weekend.

turns.inner_thought: Friday is workable if I interpret it as getting the branch merged by Friday night UTC. I can finish the remaining engineering pieces, freeze the full system behavior, and send over the pilot build once the branch is ready; packaging can follow after if needed.
turns.utterance: Yes, Friday works. I’ll merge the remaining pieces, freeze the model, and send over the pilot build once the branch is ready.
